title: Cleaning stairs, landings, balustrades and handrails
audience: Cleaning operative working on multi-level buildings, common-area stairwells, or residential stairs, under the site's approved procedure.
learningOutcomes: Clean hard and carpeted stairs in the top-to-bottom order the procedure requires, working from the edges and corners inward.
Clean balustrades, handrails and skirting boards with a damp cloth and a bucket that is changed when dirty.
Check the vacuum cleaner before and after use and position the vacuum so the cable stays clear.
Leave stairs dry, free of runs and chemical build-up, and safe to walk on.

instruction.heading: Why stairs are a slip and manual handling hazard
instruction.body: Stairs combine a slip risk, a fall risk and a manual handling risk. A wet or sticky step is dangerous, and so is a step that has been over-chemicalled and not rinsed. Working on stairs also means reaching, bending and carrying, so the worker should limit the area cleaned at one time to a size they can manage safely. A stairwell is usually a shared route, so the job must leave it passable and safe before the worker moves on.

instruction.heading: Equipment and electrical checks
instruction.body: Before using a vacuum cleaner, check that it has a current electrical safety test date recorded on the site register. Look over the plug and lead for damage, bare wires or tape repairs. Check the bag and filter, because a blocked filter can make the vacuum overheat. Check the hose for blockages and check the height of the beater bar against the floor covering. Confirm that all chemicals carry a legible label. Only trained employees may use electrical equipment. After the task, repeat the safety checks to confirm the machine has not been damaged during use.

instruction.heading: Protection and ventilation
instruction.body: Wear gloves at all times when using chemicals. Gloves and eye protection should be worn when using chemicals and the vacuum, because dust and bacteria can reach the eyes and skin. Open a window or door where possible, so that fumes do not build up in a stairwell that has little airflow.

instruction.heading: Removing gum and litter first
instruction.body: Before cleaning, check the stairs, landings, balustrades and handrails for chewing gum. Remove gum with a scraper or a gum remover, following the stain removal method for the surface. Pick up any large litter. Clearing large items first stops them from being pushed into the corners during cleaning.

instruction.heading: Dry and hard stairs
instruction.body: On a hard surface, sweep from the top step to the bottom. Start with the edges and corners, then sweep toward the middle of each tread. When mopping, mop from the top down. Give extra attention to the corners, edges and nosings, which collect dust and debris. Wipe any run marks straight away so none are left on any surface. Check that the floor is not over-wet. The floor should not feel sticky when dry, which is a sign of too much chemical.

instruction.heading: Carpeted stairs
instruction.body: On carpeted stairs, use the vacuum to remove surface dirt and dust. Position the vacuum either below or above you, depending on where the power point is, so that the cable stays clear of the path you are working along and does not come under your feet on the stairs.

instruction.heading: Balustrades, handrails and skirting
instruction.body: Damp wipe the balustrades and the skirting boards. Keep the bucket on a landing behind the line of work so you do not carry water up or down the stairs. Change the water as soon as it becomes dirty, rather than spreading dirt across the next section. Wipe all skirting so that dust, debris and chemical build-up are removed. Check the handrails for smears and wipe them dry.

instruction.heading: Finishing and storing the equipment
instruction.body: Wash the bucket and cloths thoroughly after use. Store the bucket upside down so it air-dries, and hang the cloths over the top. Keep equipment colour coded so clean and dirty items do not mix. Safety check the vacuum and damp wipe it after use. Empty and dispose of the rubbish according to the site's waste procedure. Clean the dust pan and brush, and store them by colour.

procedure: Confirm the vacuum's electrical safety test status and inspect its plug, lead, bag, filter and hose before use.
Check the beater bar height for the floor covering, and confirm that all chemicals are labelled.
Put on gloves and eye protection, and open a window or door where possible.
Remove chewing gum with a scraper or gum remover, following the stain removal method for the surface.
Pick up large items of litter from the stairs and landings.
On hard stairs, sweep from the top to the bottom, starting with the edges and corners.
On carpeted stairs, vacuum the surface dirt, keeping the cable clear of your path.
Place the bucket on a landing behind the line of work and damp wipe the balustrades and skirting.
Mop hard stairs from the top down, paying attention to corners, edges and nosings.
Wipe any run marks immediately, and check the floor is not over-wet or sticky when dry.
Repeat the safety checks on the vacuum, damp wipe it, and wash out the bucket and cloths.
Store all equipment by colour, dispose of waste, and record the job.

workedExamples.situation: A worker has to clean a five-flight stairwell in an apartment block. The stairs are hard timber with a painted handrail. A resident has left a bag on the third landing.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How does the worker plan the job and handle the bag?
workedExamples.reasoning: The worker divides the stairwell into sections that they can clean and dry safely, rather than attempting all five flights at once. The bag is moved only if it is clearly rubbish and is disposed of according to the site procedure, or left and reported if it might belong to a resident. The worker works from the top down so that the clean stairs are not walked on while still wet.

workedExamples.situation: On a carpeted stair, the worker finds that the floor is sticky after the mop, and some chemical has built up on the risers.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the cause, and what should the worker do?
workedExamples.reasoning: Too much chemical has been used, and it has not been rinsed off. The worker wipes the surface with clean water to remove the residue, checks the dilution against the label, and reduces the amount used on the next section. A sticky floor is a slip hazard, so the area should be marked wet until it dries.

equipmentAndPpe: Vacuum cleaner with a current electrical safety test status, a checked bag and filter, and a suitable beater bar
Mop, bucket and cloths, colour coded
Approved cleaning chemical, labelled and diluted as directed
Gloves and eye protection suitable for the product
Wet floor signs for stairs and landings

commonErrors.error: Leaving the stairs over-wet or with chemical build-up, so they are sticky or slippery.
commonErrors.prevention: Dilute to the label, rinse as required, and check the surface is dry and not sticky before leaving.

commonErrors.error: Mopping from the bottom up, so dirty water runs down onto clean steps.
commonErrors.prevention: Mop from the top down and change the bucket water when it becomes dirty.

commonErrors.error: Running the vacuum cable under the feet on the stairs.
commonErrors.prevention: Position the vacuum so the cable runs behind you and off the stairs.

commonErrors.error: Using the vacuum without checking the bag, filter and test status.
commonErrors.prevention: Complete the pre-use checks every time, and tag out any machine that fails them.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Only trained employees may use electrical equipment such as the vacuum. Completing this lesson does not certify you to operate it.
Electrical equipment must be tested and tagged, or inspected, under the local rule.
Chemicals must be used as the label directs, with the safety data sheet available on site.
Stop and report if a stair is damaged, loose, or unsafe to stand on, rather than working around it.

qualityStandard: Stairs, landings, nosings, edges and corners are clean with no visible dust or debris.
Balustrades, handrails and skirting are free of chemical build-up, dust and run marks.
No stair is left over-wet, sticky or slippery when dry.
The vacuum passed its pre-use and end-of-use checks and was stored with its cable clear.
Equipment is washed, colour coded and stored, and rubbish is disposed of according to the site procedure.
documentationEvidence: Vacuum pre-use and end-of-use check record
Chemical product and dilution used, with label reference
Area covered, including the stair sections and landings completed
Record of any gum, damage or hazard found on the stairs
Any incident or slip reported to the supervisor
summary: Check the vacuum and chemicals first. Only trained employees may use the electrical equipment.
Sweep or vacuum before wet cleaning, and work from the top down with edges and corners first.
Keep chemical dilution to the label, rinse as needed, and leave the stairs dry and not sticky.
Limit each section to a size you can manage, and keep the vacuum cable clear of the path.

knowledgeChecks.question: When cleaning carpeted stairs, what is the correct first cleaning step for dust and dirt?
options: Wash the carpet first with hot water, starting from the middle of the stair
Vacuum the surface dirt and dust, with the vacuum placed so the cable stays clear
Wet mop the stair first, then vacuum once it has dried and rinse the mop well
Use a leaf blower across the steps and then the handrail and balusters

knowledgeChecks.question: On a hard stair, which direction does the sweeping procedure give?
options: From the bottom step to the top step, starting at the centre of each tread
From the top step to the bottom, starting with the edges and corners
From the centre of the landing outward and then across the steps
Side to side across each tread on every step of the whole stair

knowledgeChecks.question: Why must a stair not be left over-wet or sticky after mopping?
options: Wet mops damage the paint on the balustrades and leave marks on the walls
It creates a slip hazard, and excess chemical can leave a sticky residue
It only increases the time the carpet takes to dry and makes guests wait longer
Water causes the vacuum cleaner to spark if the cable is near the wall
